name: Chlorhexidine / antibacterial body wash

lead: Chlorhexidine is an antiseptic used in surgery and hospitals and sold as a skin wash. Some people use it on the back, chest and shoulders to cut bacteria and calm folliculitis bumps for clearer body skin.

It binds bacterial cell walls and disrupts their membranes. Its research comes from surgical and hospital settings, such as Staphylococcus aureus decolonization, and no trial of its use for cosmetic folliculitis was found.

paras: It is used as a body wash in the shower and rinsed off, in a routine for areas prone to folliculitis. It is available over the counter in the United States.
Skin irritation and allergic reactions are reported, and contact with the eyes or ears can cause damage, so labelling says to keep it away from them.

angle.text: People wash the back, chest and shoulders with chlorhexidine to lower skin bacteria and calm folliculitis bumps, leaving clearer body skin. It is studied in hospitals for bacterial decolonization.

lead: Chlorhexidine is a cationic bisbiguanide antiseptic used on skin, wounds, in dentistry and on medical equipment, and it is available over the counter in the United States.[1] Chlorhexidine washes are used in healthcare for Staphylococcus aureus decolonization,[2][3] and some people use antibacterial body washes for body folliculitis.
Evidence for chlorhexidine washes comes mainly from surgical and hospital settings; no trial of its use for cosmetic body folliculitis was found.
infobox: OTC in US; some products Rx-only; WHO Essential Medicines List[1]

paras: Medical uses include pre-surgical skin and hand disinfection, wound cleaning and mouthwash; Wikipedia says 2% preparations outperform 0.5% for surgical site infection prevention, and daily chlorhexidine bathing reduced hospital-acquired infections in a US ICU trial.[1]
Reported effects include skin irritation and allergic reactions; eye contact can damage the cornea and it is ototoxic if it enters a ruptured eardrum.[1]
The positively charged molecule binds bacterial cell walls; it is bacteriostatic at low and bactericidal at high concentrations, active against many bacteria and yeasts but not spores.[1]

A trial in shoulder arthroplasty patients found neither chlorhexidine wash nor benzoyl peroxide soap effective at removing Cutibacterium from skin.[4] A study in Mohs surgery examined decolonization with intranasal mupirocin and chlorhexidine wash.[3] A review discusses povidone iodine as an alternative to mupirocin and chlorhexidine for S. aureus decolonization, citing resistance and failure concerns.[2] No studies of chlorhexidine body wash for folliculitis were found.
